title: Part 5
text: processing the worst realization of his evening, and the next the perch he'd been lounging on became a slipway as a high-pressure spray nailed him across the ribs and the cabinet was gone and the wall was somewhere his body was traveling toward at significant speed. The impact drove the air out of him completely, shoulder and cheek connecting with the lockers hard enough to see white, and he had approximately half a second to register that he'd lost the phone before the current got his legs and the floor stopped being a concept he had access to. The knife went somewhere. He didn't see it go. He got a hand on the lockers — fingertips, nothing to grip, the surface slick and featureless — and the current pulled his legs out from under him with casual thoroughness and dragged him out into the hallway proper, away from the walls, into the open water where the pressure waves from half a dozen competing jets were doing something violent to the current. He twisted, trying to get upright, and a wave caught him from behind and flipped him. He twisted again. Got his head above water for a breath, got it driven back under by the next impact. The robes were catastrophic. The long leather danced with the current, becoming a heavy fishing net — wrapping, tangling, adding weight in all the wrong places and drag in every direction. He fought toward the nearest wall, arms pulling hard, and made it approximately a meter before a pressure wave shoved him back into the swirl. Pressure waves knocked him senseless — too strong to fight, too chaotic to predict. His arms flailed wide for something, anything solid, but every grip slipped. He grabbed for a locker door hanging open and got it wrenched out of his hand before his fingers could close. The current spun him, patient and enormous, and pulled him further from anything solid. The mask flooded. It filled all at once, the cowl acting as a funnel, and suddenly there was no air inside it, just cold water pressing against his face from every angle with nowhere for it to go. He choked on the first instinctive inhale, got water instead of air, and his hands found the mask purely on survival reflex — no decision, no thought, just the absolute biological certainty that this had to come off right now. The buckle fought him. His fingers weren't working right, too cold and too clumsy, and for three seconds that lasted considerably longer than three seconds he was just a man underwater in the dark pulling at his own face. Then the clasp gave, the cowl peeled free, and he shoved it away from him. The current took it immediately. No ceremony. Just gone, swallowed into the dark like it had never been there. The water hit his face without it. He'd forgotten what that felt like — the full exposure of it, nothing between him and whatever was coming. He broke the surface gagging, hair plastered flat, water streaming into his eyes. Jets slammed him from both sides, slapping him into debris and wrenching him away again. A floating chair cracked off his shoulder. The tiled floor vanished beneath him; the ceiling overhead lost to the chaos. His robe wrapped around his legs, tangling, dragging. A jet caught him directly across the jaw and snapped his head sideways. He got his arm up too late, took another wave to the ear, and the world tilted hard to the left in a way that had nothing to do with the current. He kicked toward where the wall should have been and connected with debris instead — something solid and angular that spun away on impact and told him nothing about where he was. Another jet found his shoulder and drove him under. He came back up coughing, spitting, the cold of it biting into his face with nothing left to stop it. He couldn't get stable. Every time he found a direction, the competing currents disagreed about it. His hands found the wall. The current tore them free. He found it again — different wall, different section, his palm flat against tile for one lurching second — and then a pressure wave hit from the left and he was spinning again, the robes a dead weight spiraling with him, and the wall was somewhere behind him in the dark. He stopped trying to find it, focusing instead on just trying to stay above the surface. The hallway had no geography anymore. No walls he could hold, no floor he could trust, no direction that stayed consistent long enough to be useful. Just water in every direction and the occasional brutal introduction to something solid that told him nothing except that it was there and then wasn't. He'd been in bad trials. He'd been the thing making them bad, usually — the pressure, the presence, the particular weight of knowing someone was coming and not knowing when. He understood fear from the outside in. Had studied it, cultivated it, learned its specific frequencies and how to play them. He had not, in a very long time, been afraid. The current rolled him and he lost the surface and came up gasping with no idea which way he'd come from, and underneath the kicking and the cold and the roar of water that had swallowed every other sound in the building, something landed that he didn't have the breath or the composure to look at directly. She left me. Not a surprise — he'd understood that the moment he'd checked for his terror radius and found nothing. He'd done the math. He knew what it meant. But understanding a thing and being inside it were different animals entirely, and he was inside it now, in the dark, in the water, stripped of the mask and the knife and the phone and every other layer he'd built up between himself and exactly this. No protection. No guidance. No particular value to anything that might be watching. Just a man in a flooding hallway. Just more meat in the tank. The current pulled him under again, and this time when he fought back to the surface it was pure reflex, nothing behind it but the dumb animal insistence on one more breath. That was all he had left. Ch 8 – Flotsam The hallway screamed with water and metal. Orela’s flashlight arced wildly through the chaos, cutting sharp glints into the shattered mess around them — a locker door hanging open, water sheeting off the ceiling in solid curtains, the shape of Jake braced in a corner with Dwight pinned against him, David trying to hide his face against his arms in a futile effort to keep the back spray out of his sinuses. And still the current surged — not enough to sweep them fully, but more than enough to throw them off balance. She swept right. Debris. She swept left. Wall. She swept further and the beam caught something that wasn't wall and wasn't debris — a shape, flailing, bouncing off the lockers like a ragdoll. She didn't place him immediately — the distance was wrong, the shape was wrong without the robes reading the way they usually did — and then Leon's hand closed on her arm and she felt him go rigid beside her, and that was enough. She followed his eyes, looked again, and this time the shape resolved. She grabbed Leon's sleeve and pointed, hard, then turned and started waving at the others. Dwight saw where they were looking and moved without thinking. The water sloshed hard as he pushed off the wall, slamming forward through the current. One moment he was against the wall with Jake's arm across him, the next he was pushing forward through the water, shouldering past without explanation, eyes fixed on the shape tumbling down the hallway. He didn't think about the current. Didn't think about the water level or the pressure waves or the fact that his legs had barely been reliable for the last hour. He just moved — some part of him that operated below the threshold of good judgment simply seeing someone struggling and moving in to help. David's hand caught his arm and yanked him back hard enough to stagger him, pulling him close enough to make himself heard over the roar. “DON’T! What the hell do you think you’re doing?!” "We can't just leave him!" He pulled against David's grip, a fierce determination in his eyes. “We sure as fuck CAN!” “David—” “Did you forget what he IS?” Jake grimaced behind them, catching the light as it rocked in Orela’s hand. She didn’t join the argument — didn’t seem to hear it at all, really — as she pressed the flashlight into Jake’s hands, pulling his arm up to angle the beam down the hall with the clear intent for him to keep her way lit up. She motioned to Leon to follow her, before bracing her arms and beginning to push through the deepening flood. She had been unable to feel helpful at all this entire time, with David clearly needing help but rejecting it, and the others barely standing still long enough for her to even assess them. But here was something she COULD accomplish. Killer or not, she wasn’t going to just let someone drown not even 60 feet away. Not if she could do something about it. Behind her, Dwight met David's eyes. It wasn't a long standoff. Dwight didn't have David's build or his stubbornness, and they both knew it — a straight contest of wills between them had a predictable outcome. But Dwight held the look, steady, and something in it must have landed, because David's grip on his arm loosened by degrees. Dwight wrenched his arm back, and David finally let go. He watched Dwight half swim, half sprint off after Orela, then turned back to resume battering at the door. Someone had to keep working on the exit. Someone had to be practical about this. He put his shoulder into it again and tried not to think about what was happening down the hall. He needed to get the others out before their own altruism got them all killed. Leon made it two steps. His breath hitched as he watched Orela go. His feet planted, shoulders tense, the flicker of the beam reflecting off her soaked shirt as she moved into the darkness, Dwight hot on her heels. Leon moved to follow the rescue team but froze in place. His brain screamed at him to move — go — but the water was so high now, pulling at his legs and stomach in unnatural swirls of current. The surface was so intensely dark. The faint memory of a black claw coiled towards him, seizing his spine. He tried to step forward and nothing moved. Every inch of him had locked up, heart hammering, legs unwilling. Jake’s touch on his arm shattered the moment and he startled, eyes wild and chest heaving, as the flashlight was pushed into his hands. “I got you, man. Just keep us lit as best you can, ok? I’ll make sure they come back.” Leon swallowed once, eyes flicking to Orela’s shrinking silhouette, then back to Jake. An embarrassed nod of understanding passed between them and Jake turned to paddle after the others, leaving Leon to curse at his own freeze up. The moment had passed but the sting of it sat deep in him as he trained the light down the hall onto his friends. Orela’s boots skidded once, then bit. She leaned hard into the current, arms braced forward. Danny breached the surface in a sputtering mess of limbs and panic just as she reached him, and she snagged him — fingers locking in the collar of his sodden robes. The drag was considerable. He was soaked through. Every inch of that heavy leather robe, canvas wraps, thick gloves — a walking anchor now clinging to her arm, trying to climb straight up her. His weight unbalanced her, and Orela went sideways and down before she'd fully registered what was happening. Her shoulder hit the wall and then his hands were on her shoulders and he was pulling down — not intentionally, just pure animal logic and a drive to go UP — and for one lurching second, they were both going under. Her shoulder slid across the wall. She got her back against it and held, both hands locked in his collar, teeth gritted, the pull of him dragging at her arms with a steady insistence that threatened to twist her loose from her precarious stability. Dwight reached her first, plastering himself against the wall and grabbing her arm with both hands, anchoring. Jake was a half second behind, getting a hand into the back of Danny's collar alongside hers, and the three of them formed a human chain against the wall — Dwight braced and pulling, Orela holding, Jake hauling — working Danny hand over hand out of the current's reach and back toward solid footing. Danny thrashed against the sucking current, panic-born, nearly tearing free from the grip as the three dragged him back towards the wall away from the jets of chaos with everything they had. They got him against the wall and held him there while he fell apart. Danny collapsed against the wall, nearly sliding right back into the water were it not for the boys at each arm holding him upright, coughing up water in long, wracking heaves, one hand braced against Dwight's shoulder without appearing to register it was there. Blood tracked down from somewhere above his hairline, thinned to pink by the water. His lip was split. The whole of him slumped like dead weight, eyes barely tracking. Orela’s hands went straight to the soaked folds of his robe. The fabric clung to his frame, leather straps pinning it against him, water pouring off it in sheets. "Off," she snapped, already tugging at the collar. "You may as well have worn a damned anchor. What kind of idiot wears twenty layers in a goddamn aquarium?!" She got her fingers under the first buckle, wrenching it apart with a practiced efficiency. The leather resisted — swollen, stiff, the hardware fused with water and pressure — and she worked it loose by force of will, peeling the first layer back and shoving it into the current without ceremony. It went immediately, swallowed by the dark water like it was glad to be rid of the job. The next layer followed. Then the one beneath that, canvas and lining and the waterlogged padding that had been adding weight to weight for the better part of an hour. The robe peeled over his head in sodden layers, straps slapping wetly against her arm as she tossed them aside. "You’re not dying on me because you’re too stupid to change clothes," she growled, medic’s patience long gone. Danny wheezed, eyes half-shut, but didn’t argue. No jokes. No bravado. Just silence, shivering with spent adrenaline under their hands as nearly 30 pounds of cloth came free and hit the water with a heavy slap, slowly vanishing into the darkness below. The last of the sodden layers vanished into the current behind them. Gone. Beneath all the armor and theatre, there was just... a guy. Drenched. Pale. Shaking. Human That was the thing that struck Dwight, standing there in the churning dark with his hand still on Danny's arm — the sheer unremarkability of what was underneath. Jeans. A t-shirt, soaked through and clinging. Dark hair plastered flat. A face that, without the mask and the cowl and the whole assembled architecture of the thing, was just a face. Younger than expected, maybe. Harder to read without the framing. He was still shaking. Trying not to show it, or maybe past the point of being able to manage that particular performance. Either way, he vibrated lightly in place. Jake appeared at Dwight's shoulder, angling his voice close to be heard. "We should get back to the foyer. Hall's turning everything into a whirlpool — more room to move back there. Less chance of someone else going for a swim." Dwight nodded. Looked at Danny, who was looking at nothing in particular, water dripping from his chin in a thin steady stream. "Come on," Dwight said. Not a question. Danny came. There wasn't anywhere else to go, and they all understood that without it needing to be said. The boys each took a side and helped the soaked killer navigate back along the thin beam of light, Orela’s hand at his back, as they quietly folded him into the group. Just another fish in the Entity’s fucked-up waterpark. Back in the foyer the water moved differently — the slightly wider space diffused the worst of the pressure waves into something that only shoved rather than spun. Jake peeled off toward the door without being asked, grabbed a chunk of metal debris, and started jamming it between the warped edge of the door and its swollen frame. David grunted in frustrated rhythm at his side, muscles straining as he tried again to wrench the damn thing loose. Nothing gave. The door might as well have been part of the wall itself now. Orela commandeered the flashlight from Leon with a look and turned it on Danny, running a quick efficient assessment — the cut above his hairline, the bruising already darkening along his jaw and shoulder, the way he was holding his ribs on the left side with careful stillness. His pupils tracked sluggishly, breath tight and wet. He barely seemed aware, as if he had retreated into himself and away from the chaos around them. She could barely blame him. Leon moved to help with the door again, clearly shaken. As he passed Jake, something passed between them — a glance, brief and level, and a small nod from Jake that said nothing and everything. Leon's chin dipped once in return. It was done in a second, quiet enough that it might not have happened at all. Dwight caught it. Filed it away without comment. Now was not the time. He looked back at Danny instead — at the cut on his temple and the set of his jaw and the particular vacancy behind his eyes that Dwight recognised from the inside — and felt the last piece slide into place with the specific, terrible quality of something that had been true for a while before he'd been ready to see it. Six. There had always been six. Danny hadn't wandered into their trial by accident; he had been there when Dwight and David entered the building. He was the sixth, the numbers settled and even like every ritual trial that came before, and the Entity had known that when She set the whole thing in motion. Which meant the count had been right all along. Which meant nobody was marked. Which meant all of them were. Dwight kept his face still and his mouth shut and looked at the waterline climbing the wall behind Danny, and did not say any of this out loud. They pushed again. Slammed. Wedged. Cursed. Nothing. The roar was constant; water hammering from ceilings, gushing from ruptured lockers, sluicing down halls, but within the shift was happening quietly — beneath the roar of water and the crash of falling debris, something subtler was bleeding through. Fatigue. Disbelief. The door work continued — Jake and David and Leon cycling through angles, trying leverage points the wood had already refused, finding new sections of frame to test and receiving the same answer from all of them. The sounds of it were the same sounds they'd been making for the better part of an hour. Impact. Resistance. Reset. Impact again. But something had gone out of it. Not the effort, exactly. The belief behind the effort. The quality of each strike shifted by degrees, the force behind it becoming less about breaking through and more about having something to do with hands that didn't know what else to try. The pauses between attempts got longer. The resets got slower. Nobody called it. Nobody said the word. They just gradually stopped pretending the door was going to open and kept working it anyway because stopping meant standing in chest-high water with nowhere to look that wasn't bad. David was the last to still. He'd been running on something past exhaustion for a while now — some reserve below the reserve, stubbornness metabolised into fuel — and it had finally spent itself against a door that hadn't moved a millimetre in response to any of it. His shoulder sagged against the door, and he wiped the water from his face with the back of his wrist. His eyes darted around the hallway around them, the dark water and the debris and the five — six — people standing in it, as if the answer might be somewhere in the room if he just kept his eyes moving long enough to find it. Leon's hand moved over the doorframe one more time, slow and deliberate, fingers reading the grain like there was something in the wood he hadn't found yet. His eyes tracked the foyer in quick passes — ceiling, walls, the hallway, back to the door — as if the trick to opening it had just been missed somehow. His jaw was tight, eyes unfocused, every inch of his mind trying to slap down the question of just how much time they had. Jake had backed into the corner where the foyer met the hall, shoulders against the junction of two walls, arms wrapped around himself. His hands moved over his own forearms in short restless passes. His eyes were down, following the shadows against the walls as if tracking the waterline creeping higher. Danny had listed sideways until his shoulder found Orela's, the effort of staying upright more exhausting than it was worth in the moment. She'd let him, which said something about the state of things. He was looking at the group with an expression that had shed all of its earlier distance — watching the survivors like he was one of them now — and realizing just how little that meant down here. One hand twitched idly at his side, reaching for the phantom of a knife that was long lost. Orela kept her eyes on the door. Nobody had to say it. They could all feel it pressing in around them. The basement had filled from the ground up, patient and complete, until it had nowhere left to go but through the ceiling. The main doors had taken everything they had and given nothing back. The back door had done the same. The windows Jake had worked on in what felt like another lifetime had absorbed the crowbar without comment. The walls bled water from every seam and showed no sign of running dry. The geometry of the building had doubled and tripled and rearranged itself they could barely recognize the layout anymore. They had tried everything the building had presented them with. The building had not run out of answers. They stood in the roar of it — six people in chest-high water in a foyer that was still shrinking — the stillness between them fragile and uneasy. Silence pulsed under the roar of the water. "...Did you try the side entrance yet?" The words came out thin and ragged, half swallowed by the noise, Danny pushing himself upright from Orela's shoulder with a wince as his ribs filed a formal complaint. Heads turned. Leon’s eyes narrowed, his breath harsh as he gave a single tired laugh, incredulous. "The Entity always puts a wall there. Hardly ever a door. And on the off chance it IS..." He gestured at the swollen back door, water lapping at his ribs. "It’ll just be more of this." The water lapped at Danny as he settled his back against the wall, and he spat once to the side, shoved his wet hair back from his face. His expression settled into something that wasn't quite a smile — too waterlogged for that, too recently acquainted with the bottom of a hallway — but still showed the smallest spark of his usual dramatic flair. "...You do know those walls are breakable, right?" Ch 9 – Threshold The school had stopped pretending to have a floor. Not entirely — the taller ones could still find it if they stretched, toes scraping tile in the brief spaces between surges, just enough contact to push off from before the next wave took it away again. For the rest, it was just swimming, burning through limited reserves as they tried not to think about how close the ceiling was getting. Nobody said it out loud. There was a direction now, which was better than the alternative. Better than standing in the foyer, waiting for the moment the building made the decision for them. They had a direction and they moved in it and that was enough to keep the other thought at arm's length. The building had other opinions about all of this, naturally. The flashlight barely reached. Orela kept it forward and kept moving, but the beam gave them maybe three feet of visibility before the chaos swallowed it — water and noise and darkness pressing in from every direction. The school doing what it had been doing all night but with far less patience. The pipes were still screaming somewhere above them, muffled by the water but present, a constant high-pressure shriek that had stopped being startling a while ago and had become just another feature of the environment. Lockers banged open and shut along the walls in a violent rhythm. Ceiling tiles dropped without warning, each one landing with a slap of displaced water that soaked whoever was nearest, the spray cold and sharp against faces. It was a gauntlet, not a hallway. A hydraulic cage fight, and the school was winning. Conversation was functionally over. If you weren't close enough to shout directly into someone's ear, the water took your words before they arrived. Dwight kept his focus on his own breathing. In. Out. Arms moving. Head up. That was the whole job right now — not the ceiling, not the dark, not whatever was brushing past his legs in the churn. Just the breathing and the moving and the narrow column of air between his face and the surface. Anything to smother the panic skittering just under his skin. He wasn’t a good swimmer. Never had been. The graceless thrashing of it was eating his energy and burning out his muscles faster than he could recover. But he couldn’t stop. Couldn’t sink. He had to keep his mouth above the water. Something hit him broadside. A chunk of debris — metal, fast, heavy, the edge of a locker door catching him across the shoulder and spinning him sideways before he'd registered it coming. He went under. The dark closed over his head and the noise inverted, muffled and enormous simultaneously, and for one disorienting second there was no up. A hand caught him, painfully tight around his arm. He was yanked upward again, sputtering, hacking, blinking hard against the burn — only to find Danny clinging to him, wide-eyed and breathless, holding him up against the current. One hand was still locked around his arm, the other braced against the wall, his expression doing something complicated that resolved itself quickly into nothing at all. “Don’t drown on me, pencil neck,” Danny hissed, tight against his ear as he pulled him back to the wall edge. “I don’t want your death pinned on me unless it’s actually my doing.” It was clearly meant to sound threatening, but it ended up being somewhat of a comfort to Dwight. Even the killer couldn’t just let someone go out like that, it seemed. Orela twisted in the water again, light flashing over both of them. She was checking. Constantly. Refusing to let any of them vanish into the dark behind her. Her face was tight with effort. Eyes flicking between each survivor in turn — counting, clocking, making sure nobody had vanished into the dark between one glance and the next. The building had already demonstrated its opinion on unattended survivors and she wasn't giving it another opportunity. Danny was moving better than she'd expected, the water doing the work his legs couldn't fully manage on their own, the buoyancy buying him a temporary reprieve from the pressure of gravity against his own injuries. She noted the wheeze in his breathing, barely heard over the water, and filed it alongside the wet coughs that had started cropping up in the others. There was nothing she could really do about any of it from here, anyways. Leon had taken up a position at the edge of the group, shoulder-first into the current, methodically redirecting the debris that kept drifting in from the side passages. A cabinet corner. A floating shelf unit. Something that had been a door once and was now just waterlogged wood with ambitions. He caught them before they could find someone's head and shoved them aside without comment, jaw set, eyes forward. The building pushed back. The currents shifted without warning, tugging at legs from new angles, trying to bleed momentum out of the group and separate them one redirected stroke at a time. Ceiling tiles dropped in irregular intervals — not enough to be predictable, not random enough to be accidental — each one landing close enough to make a point. Debris drifted in from the hallway mouths like it had somewhere to be, and that somewhere was always directly in their path.
